builder_plan.scenario: An assistant chooses the wrong API or sends arguments your product cannot use.
builder_plan.change: Apply the proposed tool-selection or argument-generation change in a sandbox.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current agent with the same tool schemas and task budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Correct completed actions, invalid calls, retries, latency, and cost per completed task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: TimeTravelContainer: A Live Forking Sandbox for Stateful Agent Exploration
summary: TTC replaces session checkpointing to disk and relaunch-from-scratch with rootless copy-on-write live forking of an entire container, including processes, memory, filesystem, and network. It costs little in memory because read-only pages are shared after the fork, but it introduces a custom container runtime into the agent harness, adding integration and operational complexity. It can fail with tools whose state lives outside the container (external services, licenses, GPUs, kernel resources), with workloads that write heavily after the fork and erase the CoW savings, and with correctness or isolation gaps in a young runtime that has so far been evaluated only on two EDA flows.
rationale: Agents that explore stateful tool sessions (shells, simulators, design tools) gain cheap branching and backtracking from a rootless, unprivileged runtime, but the benefit must be validated on the reader's specific tools since published results cover only two EDA workloads.

claims.statement: TTC replaces session checkpointing to disk and relaunch-from-scratch with rootless copy-on-write live forking of an entire container, including processes, memory, filesystem, and network. It costs little in memory because read-only pages are shared after the fork, but it introduces a custom container runtime into the agent harness, adding integration and operational complexity. It can fail with tools whose state lives outside the container (external services, licenses, GPUs, kernel resources), with workloads that write heavily after the fork and erase the CoW savings, and with correctness or isolation gaps in a young runtime that has so far been evaluated only on two EDA flows.
84.1x environment cloning speedup, 31-72% memory reduction, and 1.7-9.4x end-to-end speedup on two agentic EDA flows (MAGE/Innovus, EvoDRC/KLayout).
